utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T. The Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. May I have the appearances for today, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm Tom Hannis. On behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor, Gramsci Di Fazio, Belinda Pidwell, and our case manager, Jasmina Bosnjakovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Good afternoon, Your Honours, I'm Slobodan Cvijetic, and I'm in the role of co-counsel in the Mico Stanisic case. Sitting next to me is our legal consultant, Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan, and Tatjana Savic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic, Dragan Krgovic, Brent Hicks, and Eric Tully. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. [Microphone not activated] we have the witness returned to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. I would remind you that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We are going to continue today where we left off.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: May I call Exhibit 1D10, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the exhibit comes on the screen, yesterday in response to a question by my learned friend, Mr. Cvijetic, you commented a decision adopted by the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 13th of March, 1993, and the decision referred to the forming of War Presidencies; isn't that right? Do you recollect that?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you just briefly tell us the scope of work of the Wartime Presidencies also encompassed the cooperation and coordination of military units with police forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was in the -- the General Secretariat for National Defence was part of these Wartime Presidencies.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: According to what you know, in the territory of the municipality of Sanski Most, how would you describe in early 1992 after the declaration was passed on the declaration of -- on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you said that you cooperated closely, meaning the SDA, with the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did this also include certain coordination of your defence activities relating to the armed units that operated in that area? I'm thinking of the patriotic league as the beginning of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the HVO as the starting point for the formation of the Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, we didn't have any coordination activities. If we had had them, what happened would not have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, may I call the -- well, that's exhibit, but it is on the OTP list; 65 ter number is 2422. That's P60.13, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, my friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, yesterday you commented this document. Let's just remind ourselves. In 1991 you were the president of the Municipal Assembly of the Municipality of Sanski Most; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the 1st of January, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Here on the left side of the screen in front of you it states that there was an extraordinary meeting of the Executive Board that was held on the 28th of December, 1991. As you can see, there were some items on the agenda, amongst them the proposal for measures for the Assembly submitted by the SDA branch. You'll recall that meeting, you were the president of the Executive Board, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I should be able to remember each meeting of the Executive Board, but I actually am unable to read the print. Can the letters be made bigger, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just to remind you, for example, at the time let's say that the position of the branch was to ask the MUP to review the work of the public security station item 2 to send a request to the B&H MUP about some personnel quotas; item 3 was some meeting of the council for national defence, do you remember all these points?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you look at item 5, please, on the same page. Now, you can see it, and it states that the SDA, amongst other things, proposed that a request be sent to the MUP to send a specialised units to Sanski Most. Do you remember this request by the SDA for some special unit to be sent there?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember whose handwriting you have here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm going to refresh your memory a little bit. These are notes from the -- about the SDA, I assume, due to inter-ethnic tensions to call in a special unit from Sarajevo from the Republican MUP. This was in 1991, probably that was the sense of it.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, there was no tension at that time. There was absolute cooperation between the SDA, the HDZ, and the SDS. Between myself and the vice-presidents and the presidents of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the interpreters didn't catch the names. The witness's answer wasn't recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you repeat your last answer please for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were no tensions at the time. Amongst us there was excellent cooperation between the SDA, the HDZ, and the SDS; between myself as the president of the Executive Board, Nedeljka Rasula as the president of the Assembly of the Sanski Most Assembly, and Ante Dunjic who was the vice-president of the Sanski Most Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you please tell me when the SDA formed the Crisis Staff in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDA never formed a Crisis Staff in Sanski Most. We had a Crisis Staff at the level of the Sanski Most municipality, and it was a body of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And when was this body formed, this Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The body was one of the forms of implementation of the election or of the will of the electorate. The president of the Crisis Staff, the president of the Assembly, the head of the Crisis Staff, the head of the police, the head of the civilian protection -- no, not civilian protection, but that segment, all these people were picked to specific posts. I am sorry, I'm thinking of the Territorial Defence, not the civilian protection, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And did the SDA have a Crisis Staff together with the HDZ in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've just said that that was a body representing the municipality of Sanski Most where people were appointed according to their functions. I was the president of the Executive Board of the Assembly, Nedeljko Rasula as the president of the Assembly, the head of the National Defence Secretariat, the head of the Territorial Defence, and the head of the then police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you please tell me, do you know of a person by the name Suad Sabic, do you know him? [In English] I apologise. [Interpretation] Do you know Suad Sabic?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you for the third time that I do know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what was his position in the Sanski Most municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that at the time he was the municipal prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can we go, please, to page 24 of this same document that we have in front of -- English translation page 24. It's ERN number 0110-4351. And B/C/S page ERN number is 0037-9448. The other part of B/C/S, please. Yeah, that one. Okay. If you can zoom up a little bit. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you see there that it says that Suad Sabic was the commander of the Crisis Staff? Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that the SDA had three command posts: one was at the fire station, the other at the Vuk Karadzic elementary school, and the third one in Zdana Pobrijezje; did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what you say. I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Ivan Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did he have any kind of position in the Sanski Most HDZ?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if he had any function, but he was the vice-president of the Executive Board. He was my deputy. I'm just going to comment, if you permit me. There was no Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have please another page, B/C/S version 0037-9449. And the English version is -- well, it splits. It's 0110-4351, but due to the translation, it's two B/C/S pages on one page of English version. Yeah. Okay. Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karabeg, do you know that there were two detachments and two companies in Sana of Muslim units?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, it's possible there was something in Vrpolje, this is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please now look at page 2 here on the right-hand side, and can you see what it says there? There were four platoons, eight companies, and seven detachments with a total of 1.860 members. Did you know about this, that this was the way the Muslim forces were organised in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me look at that. Is it here at the bottom where it says 1.860?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, but let me help you a little bit here. The names are Caplje, Vrpolje, Hrustovo, Stara Rijeka, Majdan, Cirkici, Vakuf, Fitovce [phoen], and so on and so forth. So we can see that there are about 20 settlements here and totalling 1.860. Did you ever talk about brave soldiers and officers of the patriotic league after the war and how they were organised?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, there were some at Hrustovo, but the rest of it you don't need to add, you shouldn't add it. I wish that it were so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, I have lost track of what the identity of this document is. Could you please help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's a diary, I believe, of -- seized in Serbia Crisis Staff, but maybe Mr. Di Fazio can give us more light. MR. DI FAZIO: It's said to be - by the Prosecution, if Your Honours please - a diary kept and maintained by a gentleman named Nedeljko Rasula who was a functionary in the SDS in Sanski Most. I can't tell you now off the top of my head where or when it was seized by members of the OTP, but that's the basic position of the Prosecution on this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A correction, please, it wasn't Andjelko, but Nedeljko Rasula.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Does that satisfy your inquiry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, but I understand that no questions are being raised as to the authenticity of this document by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We are in process of checking all these circumstances about this document, but I believe that the same document was discussed in Brdjanin trial. MR. DI FAZIO: It was. It was a controversial document in that case, and there was evidence called, I believe, concerning the authenticity of that document. But there will be further evidence brought by the Prosecution in this case dealing with that very issue of the authenticity of that document. You will hear more about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I can't wait. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karabeg, after your incarceration, you gave a statement to the AID office which is the secret police of the Muslim Croat Federation in Travnik; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In that statement, you described certain events. The full name of the service was the Centre of Security Services Banja Luka with the seat in Travnik, is that so?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please explain to me why did the Muslim side establish a parallel centre of security services under the name of Banja Luka that was seated in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you either do not wish or cannot understand. By virtue of the referendum, we decided to declare independence in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Of course, we were ready to accept all legal bodies, and naturally, the centre of public security was supposed to be in Banja Luka with a temporary seat in Travnik. Had it -- had we been able to establish it in Banja Luka, we would not have opted for Travnik as a temporary seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, did you know that in 1992 until 1995, and even to the present and the centre of security services in Banja Luka, there were Muslim active-duty policemen as well as Croatian active-duty policemen in senior positions, are you familiar with that? Just tell me whether you are familiar with that or not.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How is it possible, then, that such professional active-duty policemen in senior positions remained working for the CSB in Banja Luka during the war, whereas another group formed a parallel CSB with a seat in Travnik? How is that possible? How come not all Croatian and Muslim active-duty officers left Banja Luka and went to Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: You shouldn't ask me that. There may have been a minority which had to stay behind, be it because their families were threatened or for any other reason. This was a minority. You were killing, slaughtering, raping, and now you are asking me why. I certainly did not go from Sanski Most to Manjaca of my own accord. I was arrested, detained, maltreated, beaten, and taken to Manjaca. I didn't go there by myself. And we were not a minority. There were a lot of non-Serbs, Croats, and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were there any Serb victims in the territory of Sanski Most municipality in the Serb villages there? Were there any Serbs who were killed in your knowledge, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were any Serb villages that were destroyed in Sanski Most municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I have in mind 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I fail to understand.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we talking about 1992, or are we covering the whole period between 1992 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Between 1992 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When Sanski Most was being liberated -- well, they didn't wish to hand it over, so it had to be liberated. And it was only normal that there was combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And there were Serb civilian casualties, yes?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I say, in the course of the liberation of Sanski Most, what about 1992 to the 10th of October, 1995? This is the story that you should be asking me about. Sanski Most was liberated on the 10th of October, 1995, and certainly there were victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: To round off this cross-examination, I wanted to ask you this. I will put to you the following facts: Mr. Karabeg, I tell you that you personally were a senior member of the SDA in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never denied that. Yes, I was. And to add, I was in the inner circle of those who founded the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Together with your colleagues from the HDZ and the municipal Assembly of Sanski Most during 1991, and until you were arrested, formed your armed formations, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what you say. This is what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what you are saying. And based on what was shown to me where this person wrote, Bring in Mirzet Karabeg so that he disappears from the face of the earth. We all know what that means, dead. Bring him in dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please. Yes or no so that I can move on.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I put to you that members of the patriotic league, which was an armed formation of the SDA, and members of the HVO, which was the armed fraction of the HDZ in Sanski Most, were organised in the military sense in the late 1991 and in the first half of 1992, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I put to you that the Muslim Croat military formations in Sanski Most carried out armed attacks against regular units of the Army of Republika Srpska, and in the course of such attacks Serb civilians and Serb property was damaged?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree. Your Honours, please do not allow him to maltreat me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I don't know where you are going with this, but may I remind you that tu quoque is not a legitimate Defence in this case. You may be perfectly right that crimes were committed on both sides, but that is not the issue in this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm absolutely aware that tu quoque is not the principle only in limited situations, but my line of questions were simply to establish, because we shall have proofs along these lines, that all three parties in Sanski Most at the end of 1992 -- and the beginning of 1991 and the beginning of year 1992 were organising themselves politically, military, and on the security basis. We shall show that this witness was not telling us the truth regarding the military formation of Muslim and Croat forces in Sanski Most, and all other actions they actually forwarded in this period, which was the reason for certain military reaction of military unit which was on that territory. That's the point of all my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But that seems to at least to me to lead straight back to the tu quoque argument. If I understand you correctly, what you are saying is that if crimes were committed by the Serb forces and the Serb police forces, then they were committed in response or in retaliation for attacks that were originally provided by the other side. Now, that may be correct or may not be correct, but that is completely beyond the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you, Your Honour. If that would be the case, that the Defence theory would be based on the retaliation, but it is not the case. Defence case is completely opposite. We shall show that not only in this municipality but in the other municipality, which was covered by the indictment, there were regular Muslim Croat forces preparing the attacks on Serbian members of the community and that in certain occasions, certain pre-emptive operations were conducted fully in accordance with a -- military regulations and military law. That will be shown. So I'm not -- it's not my intention, Your Honour, to create this kind of sort of balance between the victims and actions. No, not at all. My line of questions put to this witness was simply to have and to hear his personal knowledge of the effects. Because what was this witness testifying? That nobody was armed in Sanski Most, only Serbs, they committed -- they started campaign of terror, Muslims were, you know, like, in some kind of peace atmosphere with Croats, they are defending their citizens. So that was the line of questions just to maybe try to attack on the credibility of this witness with that area. Because his testimony -- this part of his testimony is absolutely non-objective. It is not related to the facts which were actually occurred in the municipality of Sanski Most. But in any case, Your Honour, I finish my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is there re-examination, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: There is just a couple of matters that I want to raise with this witness. Re-examination by Mr. Di Fazio:

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Firstly, just a question of names. Early in your evidence, answering questions from Mr. Pantelic, you spoke about the president of the executive, and I'm not sure if it came across correctly in the transcript. There was a -- it came across as Nedeljka Rasa, could you give us that full name clearly again, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nedeljko Rasula.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Rasula. Now, can you tell His Honours, the Trial Chamber, who exactly that person was, what position they held in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nedeljko Rasula was the SDS president, and by virtue of that position, he was elected the president of Sanski Most municipality. When I assumed my position on the 1st of January, 1991, he took up the same position as the president of municipality on the same date.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thanks for clarifying that. Another issue that was raised with you by Mr. Pantelic was this: You were asked whether there were Croat or Muslim active-duty policemen in Sanski Most in -- between 1992 and 1995. You agreed with that proposition. I just want to know what you were doing, and to give the Trial Chamber an idea of where you were in that period of time. Now, just listen to whey say and tell me if you agree with this. You testified in -- you were arrested on the 25th of May and that you were transferred to Betonirka, the Betonirka garages on the 9th of May -- I think, the 9th of June; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: During that time, did you receive any information as to the numbers of Croat or Muslim police officers continuing to operate in Sanski Most? Was anyone giving you that information while you were in prison?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, if I may --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, just listen to my question, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thanks. Following Betonirka you transferred back to the police station for a short period of time and then on to Manjaca and you were finally exchanged there on the 31st of October - listen to the question - finally exchanged there on the 31st of October, 1992. Now, in that period of time, was anyone feeding you or giving you information about the number of Croat or Muslim police officers continuing to carry out their duties in Sanski Most? Did anyone tell you about that, the figures, the numbers?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, after that you were exchanged, I believe, and taken to somewhere in Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was exchanged in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thanks. Thanks for clarifying that, my apologies. Okay. And you also mentioned today that Sanski Most was liberated on the 10th of October, 1995. Now, between the date of your exchange and the 10th of October, 1995, did you go back to Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. So how do you have any information about the --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no way for me to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Fine, fine. I understand you, and thanks. But how do you have any information about the numbers of Croat or Muslim police officers continuing to operate to carry out their duties in Sanski Most if you weren't there?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had no such information. But the question that was put to me was what the situation was then and now. When I asked about the period, I had in mind 1992. And counsel covered 1992 to 1995. I can tell you that even now there are some such policemen, but at that time no one could remain to work in Sanski Most in any government body, especially not in the police. He was leading me around. I was hoping that Their Honours would curb that tendency to try to reduce the period, but he simply used the period between 1992 and 1995, speaking of whether there were murders, victims, or anything. He spans that across the three or four years. In 1992, no one had a rifle and was unable to do anything save for the incident in Vrpolje. And then he goes up to 1995. Of course Sanski Most was being liberated and there were victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thanks very much for that. I think you've clarified. And I have no further questions. Thank you very much. MR. DI FAZIO: No further questions, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. By the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, on the instruction of my client, I would address this witness. [Interpretation] Witness, my client Stojan Zupljanin wishes to personally apologise to you for everything you have suffered concerning the events you described in your testimony. This would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, just as a general manner. I don't think this is an appropriate way to deal with the situation. That's a matter that can be addressed at the time of sentencing, if there is judgement against the accused, but I don't think it's appropriate at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If I may address the Chamber with the -- in connection with the submission of my learned friend. Your Honour, my duty is to get all instructions of my client, and this trial here is a criminal trial, and it is a perfectly appropriate time, hearing all testimonies of witnesses and all troubles for the past, that reaction -- human reaction of a person who is indictment, not convicted, is appropriate. And I would outline my submission in regard to the other cases and the situations within this Tribunal where this human aspect was absolutely allowed and nothing to do with the facts and the final judgement, it's a simply human reaction of a person who is sitting in his capacity of an indicted man. That's all that I have to say on this submission. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic. Mr. Hannis, we've noted your objection. Sorry, not objection, your comment; and it's something that the Chamber will consider, and if necessary, formally speak to at the appropriate stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sir, we thank you for your assistance -- for your coming to assist the Tribunal in your testimony. You are now released as a witness. And we wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is the Prosecution ready for its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Yes, may it please, Your Honours, the next witness is Dr. Enis Sabanovic, ST-73, he is a 92 ter witness in accordance with Your Honours' rulings on Friday the 7th of October. He has no protective measures. I anticipate approximately half an hour to 40 minutes with him in chief. There are a couple of videos which may take five or ten minutes at the end of his testimony. And at this stage, I'd ask perhaps Mr. Di Fazio could be excused for the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pidwell, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Well, the Prosecution calls ST-73, Dr. Sabanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. And we thank you for coming to attend to assist the Tribunal in its work. What is your name, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Enis Sabanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1940.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your ethnicity, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a Muslim, a Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Ms. Pidwell.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, perhaps you could repeat your date of birth for the record.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: 24th of June, 1940.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, you were born in the municipality of Sanski Most; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And you practiced medicine there until your arrest in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And just prior to your arrest, you were the head of the internal medicine department at the health centre in Sanski Most; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And you continue to practice medicine in Sanski Most today?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I'm still working, involved in medicine.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And what ethnicity is your wife?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: She is a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And prior to your arrest in 1992, you were a member of the Executive Board of the SDA party in Sanski Most; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall giving evidence before this Tribunal in the case against Brdjanin for three days on the 3rd, 4th, and 5th of June, 2002?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And over the past three days, have you had the opportunity to listen to the audiotapes of your testimony in that case?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And if you were examined on those topics again and asked the same questions again, would your answers today be the same?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they would.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender the testimony of this witness in the Brdjanin trial which is 65 ter number 10013.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P61, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: There is also a proofing note dated the 5th of October, which is 65 ter 10013A which would be admitted as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P62, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: There were some documents, sir, that you talked about in your testimony in the prior case which now have to be formally admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: There are three documents, Your Honours. 65 ter 00365, which I ask be tendered and admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What are they, Ms. Pidwell?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sorry, these are simply documents that were referred to in the 92 ter package which need to be formally tendered. If you would like me to bring them up on the screen and admit them then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You see, I've read the early testimony in Brdjanin, and I recall a number of documents that were referred to. So I'm not sure which documents you now wish to seek to have admitted through this witness, that's why I think we better be careful and see what it is that you are asking us to admit.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Certainly, sir. And this may be an issue that requires clarification. Your Honours' ruling on the 2nd of October stated that the prior evidence of the witnesses along with the accompanying documents be admitted pursuant to Rule 92 ter. The Prosecution has interpreted that as being the documents accompanying the 92 ter package. So those that were listed in the schedule. And these are those documents that I'm tendering. There are, obviously, a number of other documents that this witness referred to in his prior testimony which the Prosecution does not wishing to tender simply because they are not of themselves pertinent to the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So, would you give us the 65 ter numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Certainly. The first document is 65 ter 365. For your information, Your Honours, it's an order from the 1st Krajina Corps dated the 27th of July. The next one is 65 ter 1275. And the final document is 65 ter 3424. This is one of those documents that was not on the 65 ter list before but has been captured by Your Honours' rulings from Friday, hence it has a new 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Three documents are admitted as Exhibit P62 .1, Exhibit P62.3 and Exhibit P62.2, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't have to deal with this while the witness is here, we can get on with his testimony. But at some point very soon, I think we should discuss exactly what your order was on the 2nd of October and the procedure we are going to use, which documents are coming in through 92 ter and 92 bis and which ones are not. Because yesterday with Mr. Di Fazio, Judge Harhoff said to him well don't read the exhibits to me because they get decimal numbers, and then they get admitted. Now it appears that not all of the accompanying exhibits are coming in. So we need some clarification. Some are on the 65 ter list, some are not, your guide-line says if it's not on the 65 ter list it does not come in unless there is a motion. There's also some ambiguity from our side of the room, and perhaps not on the Bench, but over here I'm telling you, on whether or not the full statement is coming in or only the portions that the Prosecution highlighted to you. There's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Why don't we -- excuse me for interrupting you. I think we should get on with the witness's testimony, and we'll sort out these matters an at an appropriate time when we have some time where we can deal with these administrative issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, in April of 1992 when you were the chief of the medical clinic in Sanski Most, you stopped working. Can you explain, please, why?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, it started -- well, I'm going to be brief. It started from Bijeljina to Brcko then it reached Prijedor. We never thought that these atrocities would be committed or that this would be a war between the three nations, between Serbs, Muslims, and Croats. I was working, and it would happened that one day the president of the SDS would come to see me, that is the Serbian party of -- the Serbian Democratic Party, and then they would tell me that I should stop working, that I had no longer any right to come to work, that the -- a different chief or a director of the specialised services in Sanski Most was appointed now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Did anyone accompany the SDS leader, president, when he came to tell you this?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: A policeman came. This was told to me in the evening at about 7.30 or 8.00, because a colleague, an internist, had summoned me. We were supposed to examine a patient together to see whether he should be sent to the clinic in Banja Luka or not. And the president of this party came there. And then when we finished with the patient, finally he said that policemen were waiting for me and they were going to see me home. I said there is no reason for that. I had my car. And the policeman went with me. One of them was in the car, the other one came to the ward. They followed me, came to my house. One of them went into the house, told me -- he told me to get into the house. One of them stayed outside. They came to the house. They asked for all my documents, my professional documents, and other documents. And all of them were instantly burned in the yard in front of the house. I was arrested. There were four of them. Two were waiting and two came later. I was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Pause, please. When you say "four of them," do you mean four policemen?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Four policemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Could you please describe whether they were wearing uniforms, and if so, what kind of uniforms they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that they were multicoloured uniform, mostly that's how it was at the time. These were young men. They brought me inside a jeep and then in a minute I was under their feet of the four of them, and that is how I reached the SUP in Sanski Most, in some ten minutes or so. They were stamping on me with their feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: When you say "multicoloured uniforms," do you mean camouflage?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: What colour was the camouflage?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Same as the police wear now, blue. Multicoloured blue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Was your wife arrested at this time?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: No. She was not arrested at all during the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Was she present when you were arrested, when you were taken to your house and your documents were burned?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. She was in the house and my children too. But they were not arresting Serbs at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: When you were taken to the SJB building, you said that you were taken in a jeep. Was this marked in any way?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: They had something -- it's hard now. I mean, it was a registered vehicle. It was a registered police vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: You've said that you were taken to the SJB building in Sanski Most. Just to clarify, were there any other SJB buildings in the town of Sanski Most, other than the one that you were taken to?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: No, not in the town of Sanski Most. There was just a police branch in the Palanka local community. But, I mean, there were only two or three policemen there. This was before the war. There were none in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: You've said in your prior testimony that you were detained at this SJB building for a period of two days. During this time, were you interrogated or interviewed?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: When I came to the building, nobody asked me anything, no questions were put to me. I was tied and taken to the toilet which was approximately 2 by 1 and a half or 2 by 2 metres, and this is where I was held for a full two days without anyone coming round. All I could do was to beat my head against the concrete wall. But I didn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Did you see any guards or policemen at this facility during that time?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I was outside very little outside of the toilet so that I wouldn't be seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And when you finally came out of the toilet in the SJB building, did you see any policemen or guards at that stage?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw them because I was taken to Betonirka. These are garages which were 100 to 150 metres from the police station. They were on a sort of hill. And this is where I started to receive heavy blows to the head, punches, and I was hit with other implements that were at hand. So by that point my left eye was swollen. My left eye was swollen for more than two months. Unfortunately, if I can add, I had surgery on that eye last year in Zagreb by doctors from Ljubljana because of traumatic cataracts or a traumatic cataract which was diagnosed in Germany, but that's how it went on -- on anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir. When you were taken from the SJB building to Betonirka, can you describe the guards or the police who took you there? What were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth -- well, it's the kind of question that all I can really say that their uniforms were generally multicoloured uniforms. But I really wasn't able to -- I didn't have time to pay attention to that. I didn't even have time to say anything. I had no opportunity to talk or to see what people looked like. This was horrible torture that I was suffering.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Once again, when you say multicoloured, are you referring to the blue camouflage uniforms or something else?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. Multicoloured uniforms, blue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: You were also taken to a place called -- a gym or a sports haul called Hasan Kikic. How far was this from the police station, the SJB building, in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: It's some 300 to 400 metres away approximately, but before I was brought to Betonirka to a garage, I was detained there first, I spent three days there; and when I got there there were some 10 to 15 people already there. Over those three days, the number grew. There were about 50 of us. We were there, overcrowded like small fish. There were beatings. Then when we were taken to the Hasan Kikic hall, the torture continued. So it's about 3- to 400 metres away, it is the gym of the Hasan Kikic elementary school, that place.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And are you able to provide any details of the guards who were at the Hasan Kikic sports hall or gym?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: The guards were younger men, policemen, in these multicoloured uniforms with weapons, of course. They did whatever they wanted at night and that was beatings and taking people out from the garage. Beating and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: You were then taken to a place called Manjaca outside Banja Luka. In your prior testimony, and I'm referring, if Your Honours please, at the transcript T6489, line 7 to 11, you say that: "... in front of the SUP building they were putting -- they were throwing, they were making more people get into these trucks. They were tied with something. Their hands were tied two-by-two so that it was -- the whole thing was horrible." Can you please explain, the people that you were referring to who were tied two-by-two, what were they coming from?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, these were policemen who were going to escort the trucks to the Manjaca concentration camp. It was not a collection centre. These were the people in the multicoloured uniforms. The people who they were getting in, who were jumping in, were young people from Hrustovo and Vrpolje. These are two villages close to Sanski Most. These were 10 to 12 young men who were tied with rope, with both hands, the third rope would tie them to someone else. So their hands were tied together first, and then they were tied to someone else, to another man. And then they had to jump in, they were hanging over the truck, falling out, but it would just carry on going. There was no care at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Were you able to see whether these men had come out of SJB building or whether they had come from some other place?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: These young men were brought from this village which I mentioned, the village of Hrustovo and the village of Vrpolje. They were brought then and placed in the trucks. Some other people were brought to these trucks from another hall in the town, and they were taken together with us who were in the Hasan Kikic hall.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Am I right in understanding that the SJB building was the collection point for all these different people?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: The collection points could have been in Sana or in the hall or Betonirka. I'm talk about Manjaca, though. Many people refer to it as a "collection centre." Manjaca was worse than the concentration centres established by Hitler. They were more skillful at doing it than Hitler. It's a fact, though, that a lot of time had passed since then, so there were people from different posts of different conduct from different professions who were involved there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: How far away is Manjaca from Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell, we have read the testimony of this witness, and I don't see any reason why you are taking him through it once again, unless there are some really important points that you wish to highlight. But otherwise, you don't need to reintroduce the testimony of this witness. We have seen it, we are fully aware of what is in there. And this is the purpose of the 92 ter procedure, as you are well aware.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Yes, I am sir. I am attempting to highlight some aspects which are pertinent to our indictment and the Prosecution's theory of the case, and I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: You say in your prior testimony at page T6489 that the police met you at Manjaca. Can you describe the uniforms of the guards at Manjaca camp, please?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's very difficult to say. There were all sorts. There was police, this was the Banja Luka police. We were brought by the Sanski Most police. There were policemen there who waited for the trucks, even in uniforms of the former Yugoslav People's Army, the olive-drab uniforms. They were standing behind. The police in question were mostly military police wearing multicoloured uniforms. As soon as it's wartime, it's the military police that is involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: You also mentioned in your prior testimony that Stojan Zupljanin visited Manjaca at T6578 lines 1 to 22 of the transcript. Do you know if he visited once or more than once?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I know that he came once in late July. I'm not sure, but I was told that he had been there one more time. I was told by the police. This was already the time when the situation had stabilised a little bit and it was not the same as it was in June, the dying and what was happening, that was outside the bounds of human behaviour. He had been there. However, those people who came from the leadership of the so-called Serbian Republic of Bosnia Krajina which is the Republic of Srpska Krajina right now, they were actually implementing a strategy of destruction and the forming of some small little state that was supposed to be part of the then anticipated Greater Serbia. So the strategy was sold. So even the policemen who beat me, I don't condemn them, but those who issued the orders, who created the strategy of how to destroy people, this was out of the ordinary. I am familiar with fascism, but this was a part of fascist oriented and fascist ideas.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Did you see Stojan Zupljanin at Manjaca yourself?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I did. Unfortunately not many times because I was there before. There was a seriously ill man in the infirmary. He was in a different stable at the first entrance, and this guy was in the other entrance. I was not allowed -- I mean, he started to talk. I was not allowed to go in when the speech began. The only thing that I heard well was the applause of the inmates who were there in that stable. I have a football team in Sanski Most in Grmec [as interpreted]. The listeners couldn't clap enough when it was explained to them that they would go home. But those who had committed something would be subject to proceedings by the military court or some lighter violations would be punished by expelling them to some third country. And those who were allegedly not guilty of anything, because in my case it said that I was the fourth in line in Sanski Most as the most conservative person out of a total of 400 people, which means that I would not be released, but that I would be liquidated.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: When you say you heard --

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Is that the appropriate time, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your permission, I would like to make a correction to page 21 line 19 of today's transcript. The 65 ter 3424 tendered by the OTP has actually been admitted with the previous witness as Exhibit P60.12. And 65 ters 365 and 1275 will receive numbers P61.1 and P61.2. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell, I think there is some confusion in what the witness told us about the incident in Manjaca in the stable with the speech and the applause. You asked about the visit from Mr. Zupljanin, and I think the witness was referring to the visit of Mr. Brdjanin, as I take his statement in the Brdjanin case. I checked that during the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I will clarify that with the witness, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, before --

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: All those who came follow the same system, the same tactics. The inmates applauded because they were hoping to go home as they were being told, whereas some were supposed to be expelled to third countries or find their way out of the prison or out of the camp. That is why the detainees were applauding. The same thing happened when Mr. Brdjanin visited, as well as Mr. Zupljanin. These were not long speeches. All of that was short, and that's why the detainees applauded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, when Mr. Zupljanin came to Manjaca on this day, you have described how you heard the detainees clapping after he was speaking in the stables. Can you describe where you saw him, please?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: As he was moving from one stable to another. He was inside a stable as I was coming back from the clinic and I saw him there. They wouldn't allow me in because this speech had already commenced. I saw him moving from one stable to another. I was about 10 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And how did you know it was Stojan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I had heard of his visit before that. I heard he would visit that day from the police. It was at the time when I had -- well, I couldn't say authority, but when the police started behaving much better towards me, as well as the warden. The situation changed because I treated both the police as well as the management of the camp and even some farmers, local farmers, from Manjaca. June was rather bad when those from Sanski Most came and when some documents arrived about me, but later on that changed. Irrespective of their Chetnik ways, they realised that I treated Mr. Popovic, who was the warden, the same as I did anyone else. I sent him to the clinical hospital in Banja Luka for his heart problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: When you saw Stojan Zupljanin on this day, was he accompanied by anyone, and if so, do you know who those people were?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who those people were, and I couldn't know. I didn't ask anyone. I was just told before his arrival that Zupljanin would come. Indeed it was him. As for those escorting him, I don't know who they were, bodyguards, I presume.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And did you speak to the other detainees about Mr. Zupljanin's visit after he had left?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, certainly. We all talked about that. Some were even optimistic as they believed they would go home, that things would be over. It was early August or late July. As a matter of fact, we remained there until the second half of November. At that point in time, they were hoping, having heard the speech, that they would go home, and that is primarily why they applauded.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Was this the only time that you actually saw Mr. Zupljanin at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Are you able to recall if his second visit was before or after this time, his other visit to Manjaca was before or after this occasion when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: The first visit is when I saw him for the first time, unless he had previously been there to see those in charge of the camp without going to the stables. That would be another thing. But this was the first time I saw him. When he came for the second time, it was far shorter and there were no discussions. But the same system was in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one question for the transcript. The witness said the first visit when I saw him was the first and the last time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Do you know if the second visit was a few days after the first, or several weeks, or months? Are you able to remember or give the Trial Chamber an approximate time --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It's a leading question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, you may rephrase your question, but could I remind you, Ms. Pidwell, that you've used already 30 minutes of what was supposed to be a very short introduction. And if you still have videos to show to this witness, then let's get on with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. The Prosecution had advised 45 minutes for this witness, and I'll be finished within that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Do you know the time difference between the two visits of Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Two or three weeks, more or less. The second visit was shorter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And when you say "shorter," how long was it; do you know?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as we could see when he spoke to the inmates, that was for about half an hour. He was there also to see the commander of the camp and the warden as well as those in charge of the camp in general.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Do you know if Mico Stanisic ever visited Manjaca, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I used to know a lot, but I'm no longer certain whether he ever was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Do you know if General Talic ever visited Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Do you recall when that was?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I think all those visits took place in July/August. Perhaps a few towards the end of June. All of the visits took place within two or three months. We didn't pay much attention to them, at least I did not. I did not prepare myself to follow who went where or who said what. I didn't prepare myself for that in particular, so there may be omissions or things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Do you recall when some international news crews came to Manjaca in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: There were several. Even some Serb priests were there, five or six young men who had come from Australia, then the CNN, some other agencies. Lots of people came, and each of them had their own opinion, which mainly tallied with the strategy of those who had begun the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I'd like now to show a portion of a video. It's less than 2 minutes long. It's 65 ter 2301. The sound quality is very bad. It's a CNN report. It has -- it is in English. It has B/C/S subtitles, and the interpreters have been given the transcript. So I would ask that they translate we go, for the English, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And while we wait for the video to come up, where is it taken and what do we see?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sorry, sir. It is a CNN report of a visit to Manjaca camp in August 1992, reporting -- a report from Christiane Amanpour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We can merely read out the transcript we have been given. Female voice: Manjaca is a military camp in Serbian held Northern Bosnia. Authorities say they hold 3 and a half thousand prisoners here including about 1.000 from the notorious Omarska camp. Pictures of emaciated captives in detention centres last week outraged the international community and prompted the Serbian leaders to quickly transfer a hundred into this military facility. Mail voice: This terrified little prisoner mumbles that conditions here are slightly better. Christiane Amanpour: We get enough food now, says this man. We were only allowed to interview two inmates and in each case the soldiers immediately wanted to know what we had asked. This is one of the camps officials of the International Red Cross say they will be inspecting this week. Indeed, the president of Bosnia's Serbs has offered to hand them control of all of these detention centres. The Serb leadership is under tremendous pressure to allow outsiders access to these camps. The proposed UN resolution would authorise any means necessary to implement that access, as well as guarantee the supply of humanitarian aid. Still, even though Karadzic himself authorised our visits to this camp, journalists were allowed less than half an hour it to assess the situation. Soldiers moved us along rapidly, allowing us to take very few pictures and to ask even fewer questions. The camp commandant insists the Geneva Convention it being respected but those prisoners we asked maintained they were civilians not soldiers. Those we saw were crammed into cattle sheds where they spend all day and all night, huddled together like animals. They are allowed to leave these quarters only briefly to a small ration of bread and soup. Christiane Amanpour, CNN, Manjaca in Northern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, you saw the CNN clip. Was that a true depiction of Manjaca detainees in August when you were there?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: By that time, the situation had improved. There was more food. But the food is not everything that was taking place there. You can see for yourselves what they looked like. They said that it was good and that there was food, but they couldn't say anything. They feared the night and the things that would happen. They would be taken out, beaten. That was -- there was a reason why they kept saying that conditions were good and that they had food. One of them once dared say that there were problems, and I remember clearly what fate befell him.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Prosecution would like to tender that video as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P63, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sorry, I've just been advised I must say it's a clip from that portion of the 65 ter number video. Just finally, could I have 65 ter 2314, please. This is also a video-clip. It's -- it's less than 5 minutes long. It's -- we won't show the whole thing. It's an aerial view of the area of Sanski Most and Manjaca taken by the Office of the Prosecutor in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could pause it there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, are you able to identify these buildings?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Not quite. Because the stables or the so-called pavilions where we were are not shown here. I'm unable to say what these buildings are. This was recorded from an airplane, and it's not a very good quality. I seldom left the building. I was only within the barbed-wire perimeter. I never left the perimeter, not by 1 metre. So I can only tell you what things looked like from the inside.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Perhaps we'll play it for 30 more seconds and if there's anything you do recognise, sir, perhaps you could say, Stop. Otherwise we'll leave it there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd be glad to help.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Was there anything you recognised in that footage or not?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: No, there wasn't. I saw a large meadow with hedges and houses, but there's nothing I can make out.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: It's fine. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Perhaps if that could be marked for identification, and we will tender that through another witness. I have no further questions. If you could please remain there and answer any questions from the Defence counsel, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P64 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Sabanovic.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Although I think it may be early evening already. I'm attorney at law, Slobodan Cvijetic, co-counsel appearing for Mr. Mico Stanisic. I have a few questions of you concerning your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before my first question, I would kindly ask for Defence Exhibit 1D00-4522.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, can you see the document?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I can, but I have never read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I will just draw your attention to a few things in the document and then we'll discuss it. These are the conclusions of the Crisis Staff of the Serb municipality of Sanski Most. You see that certain items follow, I presume?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: For example, in item 1 it states that the Crisis Staff of the Serb municipality of Sanski Most hereby adopts a decision on the introduction of a curfew on the territory of the Serbian municipality, and so on and so forth. I believe you can read it for yourself. Next, please look at item number 8. Did you read it?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Does this refer to the appointment of the acting director of the health centre, that is to say, your former position? Does this have to do with you?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Therefore, we can see that it was done by a decision of the Crisis Staff. I suppose you agree, and I would kindly ask to you pause since we speak the same language. We should not overlap since the interpreters are putting everything we say into the other language. So we can agree that you were removed from that position by this Crisis Staff's decision? We agree, I believe. I don't think we need to repeat. Mr. Sabanovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Actually, point 8 only says that Mr. Lukic and Vinko and Boro are tasked with preparing the appointment of a new acting director, is that correct? So you assume that this is the successor of the witness who is to be appointed, but it doesn't actually say that he was taken off his job by this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let's clear it up this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saban ovic, in April, as this is the 27th of April decision, did a new acting director assume your position? Can you tell us anything, judging by the date?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to say. There was a lady director, Ljilja Kasagic, she was a Serb, but she was removed as well. Then it was Dr. Dilas who succeeded her. But I think this has to do with me because the SDS president, together with the policemen I mentioned before, had to do with this. They told me -- they informed me of that decision. And we see here Lukic and who else?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Vinko and Boro.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who these two are, but I do know Lukic. And I know that this had to do with my removal.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe this sufficiently identifies the document by the witness, and I kindly seek to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D11, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before my next question, I would kindly ask for the next Defence document which is 1D00-4486.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sabanovic, on the left-hand side you have the B/C/S version. Were you able to go over the first page?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Only cursory. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go to page 3, please, and then I'll put my question. Page 3 for the witness, please. The last page. The one following that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this 086?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not you, Witness. This is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This is a standard combat report which is also an order by General Talic. In your statement you mentioned the arrival of the 6th Krajina Brigade, is that so? This is the order ordering the unit to arrive in the area of Sanski Most. In your statement and your testimony, you spoke rather extensively about the arrival of that unit; is that correct? You have to utter an audible answer.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: But you've just told me not to.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just not at the same time.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I was on my way to Prijedor when I encountered the tanks of the 6th Krajina Brigade which was arriving in the territory of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. On page 3, the last page, there is item 3. And below, General Talic outlines the reasons for the arrival of the unit. It says that the population needs to be protected and inter-ethnic conflict prevented. Mr. Sabanovic, did any inter-ethnic conflicts begin at that time?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Not conflicts, but there may have been verbal arguments among politicians. Not more than that. On my way to Prijedor, I encountered the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, let's put it this way, were tensions on the rise among the ethnic communities, as you, I believe, put it in the statement?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: It did not come about then, but by that time it may have been so. I didn't pay much heed to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I will quote your statement, you say: "As early as June and July 1991 I could sense that tensions were rising, or to be more precise the 6th Krajina Brigade arrived in our area..." And so on and so forth. This is why I'm asking you about this. In what way did the population welcome the unit?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: It welcomed it in no way. As of World War II, there was no army in Sanski Most, and it was well known that the 6th Krajina Brigade was about to come containing no Muslims, whereas all armies before that one comprised all constituent peoples of the region. This one only had Serbs, primarily those who did not hail from Sanski Most. And besides, the 6th Krajina unit demonstrated immediately that it was not there to reduce the tensions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Why were there only Serbs in that unit?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is well known when the war started and who started it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sabanovic, you were a member of the SDA; correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And in 1991, did your party and the Croatian party issue a decree that Muslim and Croatian military conscripts should not respond to the call-up to serve the military term of duty in the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: It was the JNA at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: No, no, you have to answer the question. Did they issue the declaration that they should not respond to the call-up?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You don't know, all right. So you as the doctor, did you -- as a doctor, did you help military conscripts not to respond to the call-up and not to go to the mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We are unable to hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness needs to approach the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. From what you understood you to say that you issued certificates to those who met the requirements to have such a certificate. Some people who had some sort of illness because of which they were unable to save in the army?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Those who were in the army --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You didn't answer my question.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot give you an answer when you did not put me the right -- put to me the right question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You have to listen to me. These are the rules in the courtroom. I'm putting the questions and you are replying. So those to whom you issued your medical certificate, did they suffer from these illnesses due to which they were unable to serve in the army?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to read part of the statement that you provided to the Prosecutor. "The JNA began with mobilisation in 1991" --

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Perhaps we could have the lines and the page of the statement, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, this is on page 2 in the B/C/S, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Perhaps we could have the English reference as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have to ask our case manager to open the page in English and then we will see if the two of us are able to find it. This is on page 3 in English, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sabanovic, listen now: "The JNA draft began in mid-1991. I as the head of the medical clinic was able to issue permits to military-aged men so that they would not have to respond to the draft due to medical reasons. Most of the certificates I issued were false." Mr. Sabanovic, is this your statement?

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: No, not the way it states here. What was done was that I would take the history of the illness, I would ask the patient, and they would state the history of the illness. I could have skipped that and then establish the cause of illness, but these are positions of people from outside who were stating this, from Jasenovac between Croatia and Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sabanovic, you are very clear in the this part of the statement.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm very clear now, too. So it's clear in the first and the second instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let me read further: "I issued some 2.000 of such permits."

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sabanovic, you state here: "I did issue the permits for justified reasons." It seems that for justified reasons those certificates were an exception and that you mostly issued false permits.

utterances.speaker: ENIS SABANOVIC
